articles.title_orig: 2026 elections live updates: Candidates rally and take to the airways in final push
articles.title_zh: 2026 elections live updates: Candidates rally and take to the airways in final push
articles.content_orig:
CBS News has confirmed that Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's campaign has asked his former primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, to stay away from all remaining campaign events in the final days before Tuesday's election, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
This development, which was first reported by Politico , follows a public dispute between the two Michigan Democrats, who had been expected to make a rare joint appearance Sunday at a Detroit church alongside SC Rep. Jim Clyburn to help galvanize Black voters to support El-Sayed in his Senate race.
On Friday, Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad linking US military aid to Israel to rising grocery prices, which she characterized as antisemitic. She also called on El-Sayed to apologize for previous remarks that she said linked US support for Israel to Michigan's affordability challenges and urged him to remove a campaign ad featuring conservative commentator Tucker Carlson.
El-Sayed's campaign has said it has no affiliation with the outside ad. In a response Friday night, El-Sayed accused Stevens of attempting to rehash their acrimonious Democratic primary battle, saying she "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago," rather than focusing on defeating Republican Mike Rogers.
This comes just days after Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, publicly announced he would vote for Rogers, despite Stevens reaffirming her support for El-Sayed during a CNN interview.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries joins Democratic nominee Elaine Luria in Virginia Beach on Saturday, October 31, for a final-weekend Get Out The Vote rally.
The event marks the final day of early in-person voting in Virginia, with Jeffries rallying base voters in key coastal precincts to boost Democratic turnout in the battleground 2nd Congressional District.
Days before Election Day, Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa is stepping into the ring for a critical voting bloc in the Lone Star State: Hispanic men.
Hinojosa's campaign plans to air a 30-second advertisement Saturday during Mexican boxing superstar Canelo Álvarez's fight against Christian Mbilli, an effort to reach Hispanic voters, especially Latino men, who played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 victory.
The advertisement is titled "No Te Dejes," a Spanish expression meaning "Don't let yourself be pushed around," and repeats Hinojosa's central campaign message: "Fight back."
According to her campaign, the spot contrasts Hinojosa's proposals to protect public schools, restrict data center expansion and lower taxes with what she argues is three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's prioritization of wealthy donors and large corporations.
Latino voters in South Texas may play a pivotal role in the midterm elections, spurred by conversations about illegal immigration and Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations.
It's a bloc that swung towards President Trump in the 2024 presidential election. But the key U.S. Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton remains tight. CBS News' latest poll shows nearly 60% of Hispanics backing Talarico. Texas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.
Griselda Vera told CBS News that ICE operations dominate local conversations in Mission, Texas. Some families "aren't even leaving their homes," she said, and others "are scared to call the police in case of an emergency." She thinks that fear might translate to the ballot box.
"I think that the community is tired of being under attack," Vera said. "We're tired of having a foot on our neck."
Not everyone agrees. Arturo Salas, a resident of McAllen, Texas, said he supports mass deportations and a border wall. He emphasized the need for law and order.
"You broke the law. You cannot break the law, brother. You can't," Salas said. "Why have a law if it's gonna be irrelevant?"
Texas resident Raul Ortiz, who has served in the U.S. Border Patrol for over 30 years, said the past two years are the quietest he's ever seen the southern border. While he praised the Trump administration for slashing illegal border crossings, he worried that the crackdown has instilled fear among workers critical to the country's economy.
"I think Americans want moderation. They want something in the middle," Ortiz said. "We have an immigrant population out there that is important to our society, and then we also need to recognize that we have some folks in here that don't belong in this country. We need to figure out how to get them out."
Nearly 50 million people have already voted in the 2026 midterm elections, according to data collected by the University of Florida's Election Lab.
Over 26,831,000 early voters had filled out their ballots in-person, the lab said. Around 22,863,000 votes came from returned mail ballots. In total, 49,564,545 people had voted early as of Friday evening.
The voting data does not include information from New Hampshire and Alabama. The states have not reported data to the lab.
On the evening before Halloween, Democratic Nominee for Texas Senate James Talarico spoke to a crowd that his campaign says consisted of 1,900 people.
A noticeably coarse-voiced Talarico spoke for roughly 26 minutes on the Wood Stage at Aggie Park on the Texas A&M Campus, amid rainy weather.
"This election shouldn't be about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. It's bigger than that. This election should be about chasing a vision of what this state can be," Talarico said. "Texas public schools that are the envy of the nation, a Texas economy that is second to none, and Texas families that are stronger and healthier than they've ever been before. This won't happen overnight, but a giant state deserves giant dreams."
Talarico was joined by Brazos County Precinct 4 Commissioner Wanda Watson, Texas House 14 Candidate Janet Dudding, Texas State Senate District 5 Candidate Paul Thomasson, Democratic House Candidate Caitlin Rourk (TX-10) and Texas Commissioner Candidate Clayton Tucker.
Cesareo Sifuentes-Roacho contributed reporting.
A California judge late Friday ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots or not count certain votes from alleged noncitizens, and to stop threatening officials with criminal prosecution if they do not comply.
The ruling from U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson came in response to a lawsuit filed a day earlier by labor unions and other groups, accusing the Trump administration of intimidating California election workers and interfering in the administration of the midterms.
The Justice Department has pressed officials in California this month to separate out mail ballots for roughly 20,000 people it alleges are not U.S. citizens, and has issued grand jury subpoenas for officials in Los Angeles County — part of a sweeping campaign by the Trump administration. Federal officials have also suggested for months that election workers could be prosecuted if they fail to stop noncitizens from voting.
During his rally in Florida late Friday, near the tail end of a weekslong campaign blitz, President Trump acknowledged that  "28 days of this crap is a lot," telling the crowd his "voice is … operating at about 49.2%."
"I thought this was going to be my last one," he said. "I thought this was it. I thought I could relax."
Instead, Mr. Trump is planning to visit Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two states with tight Senate races. He canceled his weekend rallies in both states on Thursday, but announced a day later that they're back on.
He told the crowd in Daytona Beach that "they called me in Iowa and they called me in Kansas, and they said, 'Sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each?' And I said, 'Does it matter?' They said, 'We just want to make sure that we win.'"

articles.title_orig: How suspected North Korean hackers swiped billions in crypto in only minutes
articles.title_zh: How suspected North Korean hackers swiped billions in crypto in only minutes
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income
North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts , reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.
“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.
North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.
A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.
The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.
The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.
The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group , was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

articles.title_orig: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots
articles.title_zh: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots
articles.content_orig:
Scientists will be tasked with deploying big data tech and underwater drones to unearth centuries of lost history under 15th five-year plan
Scientists will develop technologies such as remote sensing, ancient DNA analysis, underwater archaeology robots and artificial intelligence (AI) models for virtual restoration of excavated artefacts, according to the 15th five-year work plan for archaeology.
They will also expand international partnerships to conduct fieldwork across Asia and launch joint research in the Austronesian-speaking regions, the Himalayan area and along the Silk Road and Maritime Silk Road.

articles.title_orig: Soft power on display as China’s first lady Peng Liyuan hosts German counterpart
articles.title_zh: Soft power on display as China’s first lady Peng Liyuan hosts German counterpart
articles.content_orig:
Peng has tea with Elke Budenbender, wife of visiting German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, in bid to foster closer ties
Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan hosted her German counterpart, Elke Budenbender, in Beijing on Friday for a tea reception in a bid to showcase Beijing’s soft power and foster closer bilateral ties.
Peng stressed the rich cooperation with Germany in areas including education and culture, according to official news agency Xinhua.
She also expressed hope that people from the two countries would “visit each other more often, continuously deepen mutual understanding and foster closer people-to-people bonds”, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Two years later, Apple Intelligence makes its way to China
articles.title_zh: Two years later, Apple Intelligence makes its way to China
articles.content_orig:
Alibaba’s flagship AI model Qwen will be integrated into Apple Intelligence, after years of speculation and regulatory uncertainty
Apple’s long-awaited artificial intelligence features will be officially launched in China in December, ending two years of regulatory uncertainty as the US tech giant seeks to bring advanced technologies to its second-largest market with the help of Alibaba Group Holding.
The first batch of Apple Intelligence services will roll out to Chinese iPhone users alongside the iOS 27.3 update in December, following an open beta test with developers starting November 4, the US company said in a statement on Saturday.
The initial roll-out will include around 18 new features provided by Apple Intelligence, including writing tools for summarising and proofreading, live translation for phone calls and messages, as well as visual intelligence via camera controls, according to the statement.

articles.title_orig: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
articles.title_zh: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
articles.content_orig:
It's a mega-recycling effort: A crew of 60 men use blow torches and winches to break down a ship that had carried liquid natural gas. Tons of metal parts will be harvested to resell overseas. This photo by George Steinmetz, from the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh, is the overall winner in the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards contest. George Steinmetz hide caption
It looks like a spacecraft that settled gently onto a golden beach.
Off the coast of Bangladesh, an enormous vessel lies stranded on the mudflats, its steel hull partially dismantled as workers mill around it. This unusual aerial view of a tanker, specially designed to transport liquified natural gas used for cooking, electricity and transport, won photographer George Steinmetz the top prize — overall winner of the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards.
Each year, the Siena Drone Photo Awards highlight bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground. Here, we've selected some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs, focusing on the countries of the Global South.
In an interview with NPR, Steinmetz says he's been long fascinated by Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe, nearing the end of their working lives, are dismantled and their materials recovered for reuse. The photograph is titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal." Steinmetz sent up his drone north of Chattogram (Chittagong), along this 13-mile coastal strip, offering a stark glimpse into what this industry is like.
He was exploring the relationship between human populations and the environment for a book project and saw the industry as an extraordinary example of recycling on a vast scale.
Photographing it proved surprisingly difficult. The ship breaking industry has faced criticism from environmental organizations, human rights groups, labor unions and non-governmental organizations for its unchecked pollution, the leeching of chemicals into the sea and dangerous working conditions . Shipyard owners are wary of journalists and photographers. Local photographers initially warned Steinmetz that securing access might be nearly impossible.
Undeterred, he surveyed and photographed the entire coastline north of Chattogram with his drone, searching for a vessel that would make an especially striking photograph. He eventually settled on the liquid natural gas tanker. "The trick for me was to find the right ship, that was in a really interesting state of disassembly. And these tankers are very unusual boats. It just looked weird, like some kind of a spaceship. It takes workers a long time to break it down. And then they have to wait for the tide to be right so they can pull the pieces ashore. They have big winches and boats that they use to get the stuff ashore."
He was able to convince the owner of the tanker to allow him to photograph it. The timing of the drone photo was crucial. Steinmetz wanted to capture the vessel at low tide, when the surrounding mudflats were exposed and workers could be seen moving around its enormous hull. Their tiny figures would look like ants, giving viewers a sense of the ship's mammoth scale. He spent several days photographing the vessel, returning as the tides shifted and the workers continued to take the ship apart for scrap metal.
After graduating from Stanford with a degree in geophysics in 1979, Steinmetz had first dreamed of photographing landscapes from above while hitchhiking across Africa, often traveling on the roofs of trucks.
In 1996, National Geographic agreed to finance an aerial photography project around the Sahara, for which Steinmetz learned to fly a motorized paraglider. "It was like being in a flying lawn chair or [sitting on] the front of a spoon," he says. Drones have now completely transformed aerial photography, allowing photographers to capture the world from perspectives that were once difficult, expensive or impossible to achieve, Steinmetz says.
Today, armed with a drone rather than a paraglider, he continues to explore how a view from the sky can reveal stories that remain invisible from the ground.
Fields of handwoven carpets transform into a visual tapestry, laid out under the sun to dry. The weeks, even months, of exposure to intense sunlight gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. F. Dilek Yurdakul hide caption
Why would anyone spread hundreds of beautiful carpets across open fields, leaving them exposed to a blazing Mediterranean sun for weeks or even months?
In southern Türkiye, this is part of a traditional process that gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. Under the intense sunlight, the vibrant reds, blues and other hues gradually mellow into glowing, muted tones.
For Ankara-based documentary photographer and lawyer Dilek Yurdakul, the drone was not simply a technical choice. It was an essential storytelling tool. "I wanted to create an image that first attracts the viewer through its beauty but then invites them to look deeper, to discover the people, traditions and cultural memory behind it," she says. The photograph won first place in the contest's People section.
Yurdakul traveled six hours in blistering heat from Ankara to the Döşemealtı district of Antalya to capture this spectacle. "The first sight was astonishing. The fields were far larger than I had imagined. Thousands of carpets and kilims in different colors, sizes and patterns stretched across an enormous landscape," she says. From above, the carpets resemble a giant patchwork quilt, almost as if melded together, but her photograph captures the shadows between these slices of color.
The aerial perspective allowed her to bring together several layers of the story in a single frame, she says: the artistic richness of Anatolian craftsmanship, the scale of the landscape and the human labor that connects them.
"For me, this was a visual metaphor for the invisibility of labor. In many societies, the people whose work sustains everyday life remain largely unseen and unrecognized."
The Tumpak Sewu waterfall in Indonesia cascades from the cliffs. The drone's eye view shows Senaru Volcano rising in the distance, sending smoke into the sky. Colas Decloitre hide caption
In this photo, highly commended in the Nature category, an imposing horseshoe-shaped waterfall spills over the cliffs of East Java, Indonesia, at sunrise . Boston-based, French-British drone photographer Colas Decloitre had hoped to capture the interesting shape of the waterfall with Mount Semeru rising behind it. What he hadn't anticipated was catching the active volcano behind the waterfall, glowing red and writhed with ash, in the middle of an eruption.
"The only way to get the right alignment of the waterfall and the volcano is with a drone, as you can only be on the side of the waterfall yourself," he says. Using his drone, he could position the waterfall against the volcano, revealing an intriguing landscape that could only be viewed from the air.
A small scoria cone glows crimson amid the volcanic deserts of the Argentine Puna. Surrounded by ancient lava flows, ash deposits and wind-sculpted terrain, it stands as a final ember in a landscape forged by fire. Isabella Tabacchi hide caption
It looks like the glowing eye of a fiery monster.
It's actually a volcanic cone, the pile of rock, ash and hardened lava that builds up around the mouth of the volcano over time.
The Last Ember , by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi , is an example of how a drone photo has the power to transform landscapes into a dream-like quality. It was a commended entry in the Nature category.
The photo was taken in the Argentine Puna, a vast, remote, high-altitude plateau in the Andes of northwestern Argentina: a landscape of volcanoes, ancient lava fields, salt flats and desert mountains. The cone's reddish color comes from iron-bearing minerals in the volcanic rock, while the s

articles.title_orig: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.title_zh: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.content_orig:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said Saturday that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Khamenei made the remark on X after meeting with senior commanders of the Iranian military.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he wrote.
"The military target database must be updated comprehensively to ensure that all kinds of physical and non-physical assets" of the U.S. and Israel "are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," Khamenei also said.
Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs Waleed ElKhereiji said Saturday that people "want to bring peace back to the region" during the U.S.-Iran war.
ElKhereiji made the remark during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain, where he added that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the conflict with Iran.
“If you look at… the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear," ElKhereiji said, according to The Associated Press. "People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region."
The Associated Press contributed to this post.
U.S. Central Command released a new image Saturday of a F/A-18 Super Hornet jet on the flight deck of the USS George H.W. Bush during nighttime operations.
The aircraft carrier has operated in the Middle East in support of the U.S. military's blockade on Iranian ports.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said this week that "since day one, America's sons and daughters, serving in the Middle East, have shown relentless commitment, dedication, and courage.
"It's been the honor of a lifetime to serve alongside them and recognize them for the tremendous accomplishments on behalf of the nation," Cooper added. "As their commander, I could not be prouder, and I know that the families, friends, loved ones, and the American people back home share in this pride."
The Trump administration warned Iran that there "will be consequences" if Tehran continues its malign activities amid growing concern over a potential new round of U.S.-Iran hostilities after the midterm elections.
With just days until the 2026 elections and with war raging on in the Middle East, foreign ministers from the world's largest economies gathered in Atlanta, Georgia ahead of the G20 leaders meeting in December.
"The Iranian regime has had a choice... to either pursue the path towards normalcy, towards prosperity for their people, the path towards diplomacy. Or they can continue their malign activities, but there will be consequences for that, and we've seen the president taking concrete action," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital on Friday.
Pigott was responding to reports that U.S. officials have warned regional partners to prepare for the possibility of heightened U.S. military action against Iran after Tuesday's elections, as well as potential Iranian retaliation.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on renewed strikes, but U.S. diplomats and defense officials have privately urged several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for the possibility of new military action and Iranian retaliation, according to an Associated Press report citing two diplomats briefed on the warnings.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said Saturday that Saudi Arabia's air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone in the Riyadh region."
Al-Malki added that fragments from the drone fell "without injuries."
The incident comes as the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia.
A Republican member on the House Armed Services Committee told Fox News Digital ahead of the midterm elections that the Trump administration has a key decision to make on the future of the U.S.-Iran war as "continuing to do just enough not to lose, but not enough to win, is not OK."
Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., made the comments as Vice President JD Vance declared during a Fox News town hall on Thursday that he promises "Donald Trump is not going to let Iran become a forever war." Official and military sources also told Fox News this week that movements are being made in the Middle East to give the president options if he decides to resume strikes against Iran.
"I share my constituents and many Americans' perspective that I'm very, very frustrated that this war is not over. The way that ultimately this administration went about conducting the war, it needed to execute it and wrap it up in a very short period of time, and we are not there yet," said Harrigan, who is running for re-election in North Carolina's 10th Congressional District.
"That being said, Iran can't have a nuclear weapon. And so at the end of the day, I do believe that this was a war that was inevitable at some point, but the party that's in power and the administration that decided to pull the trigger on it is responsible for the outcome, and they're responsible for the outcome in a very short period of time. Otherwise, things get really, really difficult," Harrigan continued. "And I think we've been seeing that, both from a political perspective but also from a policy perspective."
"And so while the administration needs to wrap this up, we are not in a forever war, but we need to make sure that we're not... we keep the mission the same. We accomplish the mission. And we do what it takes to either win or come home," Harrigan added. "And that binary decision has to get made by this administration."
Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Saturday he is "extremely worried" that a new escalation in the U.S-Iran war would have a major impact, a report said.
"The second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere. We have to draw lessons from the past," Abdelatty said while speaking at the International Institute for Strategic Studies' (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain, according to Reuters.
Official and military sources told Fox News on Wednesday that movements are being made in the Middle East to give President Donald Trump options if he decides to resume strikes against Iran.
When asked by a reporter about the possibility of the U.S. striking Iran after November's midterms, Trump said late Tuesday, "I can't tell you that... but anything's possible."
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil caught fire Friday after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said, according to state media.
It was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after using unauthorized routes through the strait, the Guard said, according to The Associated Press.
Tehran has repeatedly said vessels must receive permission before traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran warned last month that vessels traveling through the strait without permission risked "destruction."
Yesterday's Fox News Digital live blog offers additional coverage of the conflict with Iran.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Mohammad Akraminia, the spokesperson of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), suggested Saturday that the war could expand in the Middle East if the Trump administration pursues new military action against Tehran.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier
articles.title_zh: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic picked a tough week to unveil its IPO prospectus .
Within days of its release, several of the company's key partners, including Microsoft , Google and Amazon , reported quarterly results that added fuel to existing market jitters around the artificial intelligence buildout.
"Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. The hyperscalers' results have "raised eyebrows" and created a new headwind in the market, which is "more doubt on capital structure," he said.
No matter the current state of the market, Anthropic was going to have to address a skeptical investor base as it pursues a potentially record-setting initial public offering in the coming weeks. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors . Investors are still waiting to see Anthropic's third-quarter financials.
Heading into this week, fears were mounting about the financial health of neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , which are facing rising borrowing costs and a dearth of lenders as they pursue aggressive AI buildouts. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.
Now investors are growing increasingly worried about the whole AI trade.
"It's a great technology, seems to do things that we never would have imagined, but how does that then translate into a viable business?" David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, said in an interview.
The Nasdaq Composite notched its first three-week losing streak since March after plunging 2.9% on Friday . Nvidia , whose graphics processing units have powered the AI boom, traded lower, along with the whole semiconductor sector, after Intel issued a weak forecast, sending its stock to its steepest drop since the 1970s.
Microsoft, Google and Amazon all had notes of concern this week in their reports. The companies have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts that came in below analysts' estimates. Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance for up to $205 billion and Amazon reiterated its roughly $220 billion forecast.
"It's been an ugly reporting season for tech thus far," Jonathan Krinsky, managing director at BTIG, wrote in a Thursday note. He described the fallout as "The Techsas Chainsaw Massacre," adding that there's too much weakness in the sector for the market to ignore.
Cash is becoming an issue. Amazon reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12-month period. Google reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, one reason the stock tanked almost 13% on Thursday, its worst day ever.
Microsoft maintained positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, but it's down significantly for a second straight quarter. The company announced plans on Thursday to raise $25 billion in bonds , as it seeks additional sources of funding to help finance its infrastructure expansion.
"Suddenly, they're like, 'We can't keep funding this on free cash flow,'" Newman said. "The worry is that basically now there's no company that's able to do this using their own business capabilities to create cash flow. It's becoming increasingly alarming."
Anthropic's hyperscaler partners are also among its biggest investors. The companies all need each other to keep the flywheel turning, a topic that's sure to be a major point of discussion in Anthropic's upcoming roadshow.
Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
A big tail wind for Anthropic remains AI demand.
Microsoft, Google and Amazon all reported cloud growth that topped analysts' estimates, with revenue in Google's business more than doubling from a year earlier. And Oracle , one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year.
Analysts at Citizens wrote in a Thursday report that the announcement "put the biggest investor fear to rest — that funding its enormous AI infrastructure buildout would require an open-ended increase in debt and equity issuance."
Attention will now turn back from hyperscaler earnings to Anthropic, as investors assess how much risk they're willing to assume and at what price.
The IPO market has largely been frozen since SpaceX's record offering in June. Biometric ring maker Oura , Australian AI data center operator Firmus and SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm subsidiary have all recently postponed or abandoned plans to IPO . Nscale, a neocloud that filed to go public in September , hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks, nor has SoftBank's SB Energy .
With Anthropic, Newman said the FOMO — fear of missing out — on a potentially "generational" company is real, and that the prospectus was "very impressive," showing 1,300% annual sales growth, 900% net revenue retention and an implied gross margin of 85%.
"Anthropic is the IPO market at this point," Newman said. "I think companies would have to be extremely cautious, if not just foolish, to actually want to come out in this period."
— CNBC's Jordan Novet, Annie Palmer and Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
articles.title_zh: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
articles.content_orig:
WARSAW — Polish President Karol Nawrocki forced his way into the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw shortly after midnight on Saturday, in the latest escalation of the rule-of-law tussle between the PiS-allied president and Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
A video published overnight showed Nawrocki pushing through people gathered at the court’s entrance, including Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge whose disputed nomination as the court’s acting president triggered the crisis on Friday.
Another judge of the top court, Maciej Berek, accused the president of physically confronting Korwin-Piotrowska. Presidential aide Rafał Leśkiewicz claimed it was the judges, whom he called “usurpers,” who had obstructed and manhandled Nawrocki.
Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”
The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management . Święczkowski rejected the move.
In a statement issued around 5 a.m. , Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”
Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.
The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.
The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

articles.title_orig: China and Chile extend currency swap for five years — ECNS

articles.content_orig:
The People's Bank of China and the Central Bank of Chile have renewed their bilateral currency swap agreement for a term of five years. This was reported by ECNS , citing the People's Bank of China.
The agreement provides for retaining the currency swap volume at 50 billion yuan. According to the People's Bank of China, this amount is approximately equivalent to $7 billion. At the same time, the volume of the agreement in Chilean currency was retained at 6 trillion Chilean pesos.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram .
The Chinese regulator announced the renewal of the arrangement on Thursday.
The People's Bank of China said that renewing the arrangement would help deepen monetary and financial cooperation between the two countries. According to the Chinese regulator, it is also expected to facilitate bilateral trade and investment between China and Chile and help maintain financial market stability.

articles.title_orig: Train Disaster Is a Blow to Spain’s Leader, Already an Election Underdog
articles.title_zh: Train Disaster Is a Blow to Spain’s Leader, Already an Election Underdog
articles.content_orig:
Pedro Sanchez, the Spanish prime minister, has called a snap election for 29 November following large-scale housing protests across the country. A month out from the election, new YouGov data sets the scene as the country weighs up its options.
Unsurprisingly, given the ongoing protests, Spanish people are most likely to pick housing as a top issue facing the country, with over half (53%) choosing it as one of their top two most important issues.
Housing substantially outstrips all other issues, with the next highest issue – the level of immigration – chosen by 35%. Corruption and fraud follow in third place, on 28%.
A further 19% cite the healthcare system, while 15% choose the general state of the economy. All other options are chosen by fewer than 10% of Spaniards.
Looking at how people intend to vote in the upcoming election shows a clear divide.
Those who say they are voting for the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), led by Pedro Sánchez, cite housing as the biggest issue (69%), followed by healthcare (31%). Voters for the smaller left-wing Broad Front (FA) rank the issues similarly, with 73% choosing housing, 31% the healthcare system, and 25% the gap between the rich and poor.
While housing is still a key issue for voters intending to back right-wing parties, they are much less likely to choose it than their left-wing counterparts. Those who are voting for the centre-right People’s Party (PP) are similarly likely to choose either housing (49%) or immigration (44%) as top issues facing Spain, with 39% picking corruption. Housing places third for far-right Vox voters, at 31%, with this group instead much more likely to choose immigration (68%) and corruption (41%).
We also asked 2,175 Spaniards to tell us, in their own words, what is most influencing their decision to vote and who to vote for. We categorised the responses using our AI-powered topic quantifier model, with the results showing that the biggest factor driving decisions to vote is stopping a right-wing government (14%), followed by desire for a change of government (9%) and the issue of corruption (8%).
Opposition to a potential PP-Vox government is a major motivator on the left, with 39% of current PSOE voters saying that avoiding a right-wing government is the biggest influence on their vote.
The picture is reversed on the right: 22% of current PP voters and 15% of Vox voters cite the need for a change of government. Voters for right-wing parties are also far more likely than those who are backing left-wing parties to mention corruption – 16% and 12% among PP and Vox voters, compared to 1% among PSOE voters.
When it comes to specific policy areas, housing (7%) and immigration (6%) are the ones Spaniards mention most. Housing is brought up most often by young people: 12% of 18-24 year olds cited it in their answers, compared to 5% of the over-50s, reflecting the impact of the housing crisis being felt more keenly by young people in Spain.
Immigration is brought up most frequently by Vox voters, with a fifth (21%) citing it as the biggest influence on their vote, compared to 6% among PP voters and only 1% of PSOE voters.

articles.title_orig: How Locals and Shopkeepers Tried to Save One Paris Street From Rioters
articles.title_zh: How Locals and Shopkeepers Tried to Save One Paris Street From Rioters
articles.content_orig:
Bonjour from Lyon, where we arrived about 3 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 23.
After too many hours in airplanes and airports, I set out for a stroll from our hotel.
I did not have to leave our block before I saw two storefronts boarded up with plywood. I followed my nose to large squares and spaces where people could congregate (Place Bellecour, Hotel de Ville, Rue de la République) and high-end stores that abound in this part of town.
In the radius of my walk, I would estimate that one in five stores is boarded-up, either from the outside or from the inside, with shattered plate glass along the street.
With few exceptions, signs indicate that the stores are open. Some, like Louis Vuitton, are fancied up while others are covered with plywood or rigid plastic (grocery stores). A nearby post office is boarded-up, as is the Musee des Beaux Arts. Photo by Elizabeth Bassett
It appears that about one in five stores is boarded-up in Lyon, France.
Several large and important sculptural fountains grace Lyon, all of which sit empty. As saws buzzed and people carried huge sheets of wood, I thought of that scared adrenaline before a hurricane, blizzard or fire, all things I’ve known at least once in my life.
So, four out of five stores are not boarded up. Parents were picking their kids up at school, shops were bustling and cafes were spilling patrons onto crowded sidewalks.
I took a few pix. I took of one of my favorite Lyon wall murals, writers of the region. It’s a sunny fall afternoon in one of my favorite cities.
There are no permits for demonstrations in Lyon tomorrow. I spotted only one Police Nationale van. I’ve read that the police will be backed up by the military if necessary. Mon Dieu.
Our plan for tomorrow, confirmed by what I saw today, is to cross the Saone and puff our way up the hill to Lugundum, the remains and museum of the original Roman city. I will certainly keep my ear to the ground and look, listen and inform myself before we set out.
Maybe we’ll just catch up on our correspondence or do our nails.
Saturday It’s nearing 5 p.m. The authorities are full-on today all over the country, dispersing gatherings, ringing monuments and helicopters are overhead.
Feels disconcerting but sort of safe. We’ll see what happens after dark when we walk about 15 minutes to our restaurant — or not.
Several professional photographers are staying at our hotel. They headed out midafternoon with helmets (army-like, not bike-like) and their enormous lenses.
The biggest group of demonstrators seems to be on the other side of the Rhone around the university, quite a distance from us.
Off to take another stroll and assess the walk to the restaurant.
Sunday It’s Sunday afternoon and once again we escaped across the Soane to do what we had planned yesterday: visit the Gallo-Roman Museum and the many remains of the Roman city dating from 43 B.C.
On our way, however, we meandered through the food market simply because it’s such a joy to see the offerings. What we found, between the oysters, olives and roasting chickens, were about a dozen camo-clad soldiers with AK 47s. Unlike the police of yesterday who seemed tense and on edge, they looked less menacing than bored.
After our cultural outing and a lazy Sunday lunch, we wandered the streets. Shops are still boarded up, and there’s some new damage to windows. But people are returning to the streets, musicians playing and vacationing families fill the sidewalks. I’ll be interested to see what the first day of the work week looks like tomorrow.
The local media describes Lyon yesterday as a cat-and-mouse game. Tear gas and water cannons drove demonstrators to ground only to have them reappear a few blocks or a half mile away. This went on across the Rhone, much of it near the university, from midmorning until after dark. When we walked home from dinner, around 9 p.m., the hundreds of flashing blue police lights we had seen a few hours earlier were gone along with barriers across the roads.
Bonus, I think the rain has stopped. Hoping there is nothing more to report!

articles.title_orig: Oil company earnings skyrocket — again
articles.title_zh: Oil company earnings skyrocket — again
articles.content_orig:
A pump jack operates at sunset in the Permian Basin near Loving, N.M., on Tuesday, May 20, 2025. Susan Montoya Bryan/AP hide caption
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.
Oil companies made billions this quarter, they told investors on calls this week. ExxonMobil earned $15.4 billion, more than doubling its earnings compared to this time last year.
Shell nearly doubled its own earnings, at $10.8 billion.
Chevron's were up 180%, at $9.9 billion.
Together, the three companies pulled in just over $36 billion this quarter.
As with the soaring profits oil companies recorded last quarter , it's largely due to the war in Iran disrupting the global oil supply. Less oil is moving through the Middle East, so the oil in other parts of the world has become much more valuable.
Brent crude is now trading around $113 a barrel . For context, before the war began, it was about $70 a barrel.
Meanwhile, demand for oil and refined products like gasoline, diesel and heating oil hasn't changed much. People still need them to heat homes , drive cars, run tractors and truck everything we buy around the country.
Dan Pickering, founder of the financial services firm Pickering Energy Partners, says that big oil companies are profiting as they meet that demand. " The majors are able to sell their barrels that they produce in the U.S. or Latin America or Europe for much higher prices," he said. "So the Middle East's loss is generally the gain of oil and gas companies in the U.S. and Europe."
On their earnings calls, oil company executives said a good chunk of their profits were going to their shareholders through dividends and stock buybacks. Shell's buyback was one of their biggest ever. Exxon announced its highest-ever quarterly dividend.
But for the most part, Pickering says, these companies are in a wait-and-see stance — they're not really spending that money on things like new drilling projects, because they know they're in an unusual moment.
"This is a period where the high prices are driven more by geopolitical events than anything else," he said. Since it's hard to predict how long those will last, he continued, "You put the money in the bank and watch to see what happens as we move into 2027."
Pickering says this makes sense because oil is a cyclical industry — prices move up and down. Companies want to hold onto their cash when times are good so they can insulate themselves when they're not so good.
A supply shock, amid two ongoing wars
The rising cost of oil has pushed up what drivers pay at the pump. Gasoline now costs about $1.20 more per gallon than it did a year ago, according to AAA . Diesel hit a record high in September , and is still close to that high.
Exxon CEO Darren Woods was one of the few to directly address the issue on an earnings call, saying, "We recognize the impact high prices have on people's lives and economic growth."
Exxon's solution, he said, is to boost production. " With products in short supply, our teams have done everything they can to keep prices down by maximizing production," he said.
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth made a similar point, telling investors, " What we can do is what we can control, and that's help consumers get as much as they possibly can out of our systems."
On these calls, executives from all the companies pointed out that they're dealing with a massive supply shock. The war in Iran, as well as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries , have taken a lot of global refining capacity offline.
The executives indicated that they don't see the situation changing anytime soon.
"If you'd asked me six months ago, would I have thought that oil prices were going to be where they are today — no," Shell CEO Wael Sawan said on his company's call. "Personally, I thought we were at a high there, and we were essentially looking at what was going to be a temporal spike."
But because the war has gone on this long, global oil reserves are at much lower levels. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at low levels; Europe released some of its crude oil and diesel.
"We're now seeing more and more structural stability in that higher oil price simply because we are seeing that inventory levels are being drawn down very quickly, and it's going to take quite some time to be able to refill that inventory," Sawan continued.
Democrats in both chambers of Congress have called for a tax on windfall profits — excess profits that come about because of geopolitical forces outside of their control, not because of innovation. Bills introduced this spring would return some of those profits to Americans through tax rebates.
Earlier this year, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who sponsored a windfall tax bill in the Senate, said he hopes it will also spotlight how climate-friendly renewable energy is increasingly more cost-competitive than fossil fuels . " Wind, solar, and battery power, they're not raising their prices," Whitehouse told NPR at the time.
Isabella Weber, an economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, has studied how windfall taxes worked in other countries. She says windfall taxes are a way to bridge the gap between what the oil companies make and what most people pay for that oil.
"The companies that are running this essential sector have been reaping record profits amidst the worst energy supply crisis that we have had in several decades," she said. "This is a contradiction that, I think, raises fundamental questions about how we organize our economy, how we organize our society, who benefits, who loses."
"When emergencies generate massive windfall profits," she continued, it creates "this crazy situation where the worst of times ends up being the best of times, which is problematic on a deeper level."
While the oil executives didn't mention windfall taxes on this week's calls, last quarter, Exxon's Woods called them a " misguided policy ." He said they penalize companies that are trying to be successful in a volatile industry.
As the midterms approach, the Trump administration has taken measures to bring down the price of fuel, particularly diesel, including temporarily loosening federal rules for dyed diesel, which is used in farming, and lifting sanctions against Russia to allow more diesel to enter the world market.
But these efforts are unlikely to bring down U.S. prices — the amount of fuel Russia can release would make up only a small portion of U.S. daily demand, and dyed diesel is still not accessible to most drivers.
In any case, significantly lower prices are unlikely to materialize by Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: In 28 years of walking, Karl Bushby overcame jungle, desert and red tape. He's home
articles.title_zh: In 28 years of walking, Karl Bushby overcame jungle, desert and red tape. He's home
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Karl Bushby has spent 28 years walking home, but as he approaches the finish Monday, it’s not clear he's ready for the audacious journey to end.
Pushing a cart loaded with camping gear up a busy country road in northern England about 30 miles (50 kilometers) from the finish line, Bushby was uncertain of the future, anxious about the prospect of living in his mom’s basement and facing an identity crisis.
“My purpose and reason for living is about to end,” he said. “It’s going to be difficult … trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”
Bushby, 57, was just shy of 30 when he entered the unknown at the tip of South America on Nov. 1, 1998. Since then, he has walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents, navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam — a generous description of his technique — across the Caspian Sea and English Channel. He has battled almost every type of element and terrain imaginable through 30 foreign countries to get back to where he started half a lifetime ago.
Swampy jungle, scorching desert and frozen tundra slowed him down, but mountains of red tape helped turn what was supposed to be a 12-year trek into the epic he has dubbed the “Goliath Expedition.”
It’s taken nearly three times as long for Bushby to return to his mother, Angela, in Hull, as it took the hero in “ The Odyssey ” to make it back to his wife, Penelope, in Ithaca.
“Odysseus was a bit of an amateur,” Bushby quipped. “But, you know, I’ll cut him some slack — I haven’t met any giant Cyclops.”
The real world provided plenty of menaces of its own: there was a standoff with a polar bear; he floated through crocodile-infested waters to avoid a guerrilla war in Colombia; a mob attacked him in Peru; and he was rescued by helicopter from an ice floe drifting out to sea.
The former British paratrooper's mission was sparked by a birthday card from his father, Keith, in the mid-90s. Keith, an Army veteran himself, mentioned an argument special forces troops once had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels.
Bushby drew a continuous line on a map across Europe and Asia to North America and — instead of going to New York — carried on straight down to the tip of Chile.
“And that was it,” he said. “With that under my skin, there was no going back.”
Explorers have long circled the planet by boat, plane, balloon, bicycle and even on foot. But most walkers have relied on transport to cross oceans.
Bushby imposed two strict rules for his journey: transportation could not be used to move forward and he had to return home on foot.
He set out with $500 and soon found himself fighting hurricane-force winds on the Patagonian Steppe. He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America, in 2001 and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama.
After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, he had a near-death plunge into freezing waters and they nearly lost all their supplies. After managing the rare crossing, they were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.
It took almost 10 years to get through Russia because of visa issues and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.
With each setback, he would retreat to the U.S. or Mexico, where living was much cheaper, and wait for his next chance to return to the point where he left off.
He was trailed by police through China, had a lengthy setback from the pandemic and was forced to swim 31 days across the Caspian Sea because geopolitical problems had closed off Russia and Iran. He is not a good swimmer and relied on a flotation vest and wetsuit as he plodded backward by flapping his arms in a technique he calls “floatimming,” a hybrid of floating and swimming.
Europe presented its own challenges, with 90-day limits on visits that forced him to travel in three-month chunks.
Romance has also intervened. He spent seven years with a Colombian woman, and three with a woman from Japan. Each relationship ended in heartbreak that seemed fated by such an itinerant lifestyle.
It's been tough on his family. Bushby has a son from an early marriage to a Belfast woman that ended in divorce. His son mostly grew up without him and is now in his mid-30s. His father met him on the beach in Dover when he crossed the channel, but Bushby hasn't seen his mother in a decade, which adds to the trepidation about his return.
He has been helped by a shifting group of sponsors that have come and gone as the trip dragged on and fortunes tumbled in the 2008 financial crisis. For the past 16 years, he has relied mainly on a production company founded by “House of Cards” creator Beau Willimon and music producer Jordan Tappis, who are backing a documentary in the works by filmmaker Werner Herzog.
It has been the kindness of countless strangers, though, that has buoyed and propelled him throughout, particularly from those who have the least to offer.
He's been welcomed into shacks assembled from car parts, nursed back to health from a bad stomach infection by a Peruvian doctor's family, and fed countless meals of just rice and water by people seeking nothing in return.
“I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he said. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country has been the same response.”
There have been endless stretches of loneliness that have made his final push almost surreal as word spreads of his passage through the rolling green fields that lead to his native Yorkshire. Big rigs literally blowing past him on the road near the town of Market Rasen on Wednesday tooted their horns, drivers waved and a group of motorcyclists stopped to take selfies.
Howard Denton pulled his car over and couldn't understand how a couple of cyclists he had spoken with briefly hadn't taken note of their fellow traveler.
“I said to them, ’Did you see that bloke who’s walked around the world?'” Denton said. “They said, ‘No.’ They didn’t think of asking him where he was going. I just couldn’t believe how stupid they were. I think he’s incredible. I think he’s amazing.”
With each mile, the end draws closer.
When Bushby started out, he looked like Kurt Cobain and even inspired an internet mock conspiracy that the late Nirvana leader was still alive, and walking around the world under a pseudonym.
He's more weathered today, softer in the midsection and has a salty beard. But his bright blue eyes, blond hair and tan belie his age.
He may not know what lies ahead but one thing is certain: he won't miss the thousands of steps he takes each day.
“I’m not doing it because I like walking,” he said. “It’s a means of getting somewhere.”

articles.title_orig: How man's Halloween house display has become bittersweet tradition
articles.title_zh: How man's Halloween house display has become bittersweet tradition
articles.content_orig:
As people up and down the country look forward to celebrating Halloween this evening, one Greater Manchester man takes the festivities further than most.
Dave Barron, 61, from Bramhall, in Greater Manchester, has been decorating his home for Halloween every year since 2011, and has been preparing this year's Back to the Future-themed display since May.
Dave's efforts are all a tribute to his late wife, Catherine. Accepting donations from Halloween visitors, he has raised more than £55,000 for the Macmillan cancer charity, which cared for Catherine before she died in 2020.
"Halloween is emotional for me," Dave said. "I miss Catherine tremendously. She'd think I'm an absolute lunatic, but she was always a big part of it and I think she'd be really proud."
"I have been working on this year's Halloween display since May," he said. "And it does cost me a bit.
"But It's a small price to pay if it helps people who are suffering with cancer."
"Within the last decade it's just got it bigger and bigger and bigger," Dave said of his Halloween extravaganzas."
Dave put on a Doctor Who-themed display last year, but said this year's had been the most challenging project yet.
"This has probably been our most ambitious challenge in all the years we've done it," he said.
"I thought building a Dalek last year was bad enough, but the car we built this year has got that many angles and twists and turns on it.
"But we've got there. We started around end of May and we've been working on it pretty much ever since, weather-permitting."
Dave has been helped by his 27-year-old daughter Sarah and other family members and friends.
He also hands out more than 500 sweets, donated by his local Tesco, during each event.
"There's so many people, from the timber company, to the tyre company, to a friend who makes our banners, to everyone else who has chipped in, lending us instruments, donating costumes," he said.
Dave said he was particularly touched when a stranger responded to his Facebook appeal looking for a 1981 DeLorean DMC-12.
"I wanted to take measurements to make it as realistic as possible, so we could build it to size," Dave said.
"A lady wrote back to me almost instantly and she said my husband has one, he's out in it at the moment.
"He offered to come to our house from his home in Poynton and left the car with us for the day.
"It's people stepping in like that that shows you how far community can stretch."
Dave also said he was hoping to be paid another visit from Salford comedian, actor and singer Jason Manford, who has become a regular attendee over the years.
"They are aiming to come this year," Dave said. "They have their own party and they tend to come a little bit later on."
Dave said while his displays were to honour his wife's legacy, he felt proud to be able to know he was helping others.
"When I sit back and I look at what we've done, it actually is very, very emotional," he added.

articles.title_zh: China joins global race to reawaken brain-injury patients through ultrasound therapy
articles.content_orig:
Chinese researchers have reported early promising results, as scientists worldwide explore ways to restore consciousness without invasive surgery
After spending three months in a coma following a brain haemorrhage, a patient in China has regained the ability to speak, eat and walk with support – part of an early clinical trial using targeted sound waves to help “wake up” severely damaged brains, according to state media.
The technology, developed by a coalition including the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, used focused ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep within the brain without requiring invasive surgery or implanted electrodes, state broadcaster CCTV reported earlier this week.

articles.title_orig: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.title_zh: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Big Tech's brutal week had one clear epicenter. Alphabet ( GOOGL ) lost $468 billion in market value this week, more than SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia combined.
That was the Google parent's worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $552 billion in the week of Jan. 27, 2025, when China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet's previous worst was about $386 billion in the week ended June 26.
Most of the damage came Thursday, when Alphabet lost $475 billion in a single session after its third quarter results . Friday's slide wiped out the gains the stock had made earlier in the week.
October was even worse. Alphabet shed about $758 billion in market value this month, the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company. Only SpaceX ( SPCX ) has lost more, about $822 billion in July. Alphabet's October loss is nearly double its previous worst month, about $420 billion in February 2025.
In percentage terms, the stock fell nearly 19% in October, its worst month since it went public in 2004. Its previous worst was an 18.5% drop in November 2008. For the week, it fell nearly 13%, its worst since August 2011.
The selloff has left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade .
SpaceX, Intel ( INTC ) and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week. Intel fell as much as 30% Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades . Amazon ( AMZN ) shed about $80 billion for the week after reporting results Thursday. Some software names fell harder in percentage terms, with ServiceNow ( NOW ) and Fortinet ( FTNT ) down roughly 25% to 34%.
Not all of that money left the market. Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Tesla ( TSLA ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) added more than $300 billion in combined value, even as the Magnificent 7 stumbled .
UBS's chief investment office argued against heading for the exits. "Further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote Friday. "We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech."
The close settled it. October goes down as Alphabet's worst month since its IPO, in dollars and in percentage terms. The stock finished the week about $7 above the roughly $273 level it would have needed to take Nvidia's weekly record.

articles.title_orig: Phantom Blade Zero Draws 700,000+ Steam Players Within 24 Hours of Launch
articles.title_zh: Phantom Blade Zero Draws 700,000+ Steam Players Within 24 Hours of Launch
articles.content_orig:
Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review . That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.
However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.
Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced , which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.
The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.
Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review , then check out our list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks we wish we knew before starting the game. Then check out our breakdown of the requirements to see the best ending in the game .

articles.title_orig: On board a Spanish high-speed train in the aftermath of the system’s latest catastrophe
articles.title_zh: On board a Spanish high-speed train in the aftermath of the system’s latest catastrophe
articles.content_orig:
URDA, SPAIN – A prominent Oklahoma City artist and arts community leader is missing in Spain following a high-speed train crash that has so far claimed at least 69 lives and left his husband – along with dozens of others – badly injured.
Fernando Calvillo currently serves as the Community Relations Director for the Oklahoma Visual Arts Coalition (OVAC) and lives in OKC with his husband, artist and jewelry designer Lawrence Naff .
The two were in Spain for a vacation this week and were on a high-speed passenger train traveling through Urda in the Spanish state of Toledo when their train collided with a separate stationary train Wednesday night, killing more than 60 people aboard and leaving a chaotic scene that was still being actively searched late Thursday.
Naff sustained serious injuries to his legs and was taken into surgery, but no contact has yet been made with Calvillo, who was seated next to Naff on the train at the time of the collision.
Calvillo’s family, friends, and OKC community are now working to spread the word, hoping that communication lines and networks from Oklahoma to Spain and Mexico (Calvillo retains dual US and Mexican citizenship) may help someone locate him.
According to Spanish news outlet El Semanal de la Mancha *, Calvillo and Naff were in Spain intending to celebrate the birthday of Calvillo’s cousin, Rodrigo Hernández, who spoke to the outlet about the search and the multi-continent effort to coordinate communication.
Hernández said that a signal from Calvillo’s Apple Watch was briefly located at the crash site before being lost, but that no other communications, device signals, or contact have been made since.
He also confirmed Naff’s condition in a hospital in the city of Alcázar de San Juan, saying that Naff was stable, conscious, and recovering from surgery.
“The truth is, the team here at this hospital did a wonderful job,” Hernández told the outlet.
Since the news reached Oklahoma City, the local arts community has come together to spread support for the artists’ families and their remarkably large networks of close friends, collaborators, and fans.
“They’re amazing people,” said Karis Chambers, an OKC-based artist and former OVAC team member that worked closely alongside Calvillo. “It’s truly a nightmare.”
Social media networks saw dozens of posts and shares Thursday helping to raise awareness of the search for Calvillo and the phone numbers – an American number and a separate Mexican number – that have been designated for any information regarding his whereabouts or condition.
Friends and family are asking for anyone with information to call +1 405 836 2880 in the US or +52 449 222 864 in Mexico
“My world has pretty much come to a halt and I think many other lives in the arts community across the state are in a similar state,” Chambers told Free Press . “We are just waiting and holding onto hope that he is out there and alive. The community has essentially been trading information back and forth to update people and make sure everyone has accurate and up to date info on how they can help.”
“Simply put, Fern and Lawrence are the best of us,” added Oklahoma City-based musician and longtime friend Chase Kerby. “Both have never been anything less than welcoming and warm.”
This is a developing story. Free Press will provide more information regarding this event and ensuing investigation as it becomes available.
*The report from El Semanal de la Mancha was published online in Spanish and was read using Google Translate. Information, detail, and nuance can be lost in translation.
Brett Fieldcamp is the owner and Editor in Chief of Oklahoma City Free Press. He has been covering arts, entertainment, news, housing, and culture in Oklahoma for nearly two decades and served as Arts & Entertainment Editor before purchasing the company from founder Brett Dickerson in 2026.
He is also a musician and songwriter and holds a certification as Specialist of Spirits from The Society of Wine Educators.

articles.title_orig: Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Oman has rescued 25 crew members from a burning crude oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz as ships continue to be targeted in the besieged waterway .
The Omani Maritime Security Centre said in a statement on Friday that it had evacuated the people on board the RITI merchant ship. Oman said the vessel was flying the Panamanian flag, and the tracking website MarineTraffic identified it as a crude oil tanker.
The incident came as Iran said four tankers attempting to use “unauthorised routes” to cross the Strait of Hormuz were halted.
It is unclear whether one of the vessels was the tanker whose crew Omani maritime authorities evacuated.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said all four vessels were carrying oil and that the ships had been halted following “incidents” or after hitting mines.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement on Friday.
Hours later, the IRGC said two more tankers – each carrying more than two million barrels of oil – “exploded and caught fire” as a result of hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorised route”.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Navy said on Friday that it struck and destroyed an unmanned enemy craft to the east of the strait.
Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission.
It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to transit Hormuz without authorisation would face “destruction”.
Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.
The US military denies the naval mine claims. On Friday, United States Central Command chief Brad Cooper said the Strait of Hormuz’s “internationally recognised primary transit routes” had been successfully cleared of Iranian sea mines.
Shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is operating at about 70 percent below pre-war levels, the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday.
